name: The four elements (earth, air, fire, water)
plain_explanation: Empedocles proposed that everything is made from just four everlasting basic substances -- earth, air, fire, and water -- mixed together in different proportions, rather than from a single substance as the Milesians and Heraclitus had thought.
precise_definition: Empedocles' doctrine that earth, air, fire, and water are each everlasting and unchanging in themselves, but can be mixed in varying proportions by the opposed forces of Love and Strife to produce all the changing compound substances observed in the world.
why_it_mattered: Russell calls this a 'statesmanlike compromise' among the Milesians' and Heraclitus's single-substance theories, and notes that 'the chemistry of the ancients stopped dead at this point,' remaining the standard framework until the rise of Islamic alchemy centuries later.
historical_origin: Original to Empedocles, though the term 'element' itself was not used by him.
examples: All complex substances in the world as varying mixtures of the four elements
competing_positions: Thales' water, Anaximenes' air, and Heraclitus's fire as single primal substances
influence_on_later_thinkers: Remained the basic ancient and medieval theory of matter for roughly two thousand years, until superseded by early chemistry.
